pos: n. (the Mesopotamian empire on the upper Tigris — the rod of God's anger against Israel, and the rod He afterward broke)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Ashshur, Asshur — at once the second son of Shem (Gen 10:22), the national god, the capital city, and the land. The Greek Assyria comes through the same name.
biblical_def: Assyria is the first world empire Scripture sets over against the covenant people, and Isaiah gives the doctrine of it in one line: “O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation” (Isa 10:5). The empire that deported the ten tribes was a tool in the hand of God — not a rival power He was forced to tolerate, but an instrument He raised, aimed, and afterward burned, “for he saith, By the strength of my hand I have done it” (Isa 10:13), and the axe that boasts against the hand that swings it is broken for its boasting. The great fact of Assyrian history in the Bible is 2Ki 17:6: Samaria taken, Israel carried away, settled in Halah and Habor and the cities of the Medes, and never restored as a kingdom. Judah, spared by a single night's judgment on Sennacherib's camp — “the angel of the LORD went forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand” (Isa 37:36) — learned nothing from it, and went to Babylon a century later. Yet Assyria is not left under sentence only. Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, and Isaiah sees a day when the LORD will say, “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance” (Isa 19:25) — the empire of the rod brought in among the worshippers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives Assyria as an ancient kingdom of Asia, on the Tigris, whose capital was Nineveh, and derives the name from Asshur, son of Shem.
webster_full: ASSYRIA, n. An ancient kingdom of Asia, lying east of the Tigris, named from Asshur, the son of Shem.
Its capital was Nineveh, a city of exceeding greatness, built by Nimrod or Asshur.
Under Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser and Sennacherib it subdued Syria, Samaria and the coast, and threatened Jerusalem.
The ten tribes were carried thence into captivity in the ninth year of Hoshea.
The empire fell to the Chaldeans and Medes, and Nineveh was destroyed, as Nahum and Zephaniah foretold.
scriptures: Isa 10:5
O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation.
In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.
Then the angel of the LORD went forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses.
Whom the LORD of hosts shall bless, saying, Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance.
corruption_summary: Empires are read as autonomous political forces and Israel's fall as ordinary geopolitics; Isa 10 says the empire was a rod God held, which makes the whole account one of covenant judgment, not power politics.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern account of the fall of Samaria is a study in Iron Age power: Assyrian siege technology, deportation policy, tribute economics. Every fact of it may be granted, and Isaiah still contradicts the account, because Isaiah names the agent. Assyria is a rod, and a rod does not decide where it falls. This is the doctrine of providence applied to the hardest case — God ordains the wicked act of a wicked empire, is not the author of its wickedness, and holds it fully accountable for what He ordained it to do. Isa 10:12 puts both halves side by side: God will punish “the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria” after He has performed His whole work through him. To lose either half is to lose the passage.

The second corruption runs the other way, among Christians: treating Assyria as a monster with no possible mercy. Jonah went to Nineveh precisely because mercy was on offer, and resented it. Isa 19:25 goes further than Jonah could have borne — Egypt called “my people” and Assyria “the work of my hands”, terms elsewhere reserved for Israel. The gospel later broke open on that promise. The nation God uses as a rod today is a nation to whom He may yet send preachers, and the church that cannot pray for its persecutors has not read the twelve prophets.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Ashshur (H804), Asshur, Assyria; shebet (H7626), a rod; galah (H1540), to carry into exile.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Ashshur (H804) — Asshur; the son of Shem, the god, the city, and the empire, all one name.
Hebrew shebet (H7626) — a rod, a tribe, a sceptre; the instrument Assyria is called in Isa 10:5.
Hebrew matteh (H4294) — a staff; the parallel term in the same verse, the same point twice.
Hebrew galah (H1540) — to uncover, to carry away captive; the verb of the deportation of the ten tribes.
Hebrew ma'aseh yaday — “the work of my hands”; the astonishing title given Assyria in Isa 19:25.
usage: “O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger” — the empire named as an instrument.
“Carried Israel away into Assyria” — the end of the northern kingdom.
“Assyria the work of my hands” — the rod brought in among the worshippers.

pos: n. pl. (the people of southern Babylonia — the nation God raised to destroy Jerusalem, and, in Daniel, the caste of Babylon's wise men)
etymology: From Hebrew Kasdi or Kasdim, Chaldeans, of uncertain origin; the KJV renders the same word both “Chaldeans” and, in Gen 11:31, “Chaldees”. The Greek Chaldaios follows the Hebrew.
biblical_def: The Chaldeans carry two senses in Scripture and both matter. Ethnically and politically they are the people of southern Mesopotamia who came to rule Babylon, and Habakkuk records the LORD's answer to a prophet complaining about violence in Judah: “lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs” (Hab 1:6). It was an answer that appalled him — how can a holier God use a filthier nation? — and the whole of Habakkuk 2 is the reply. These are the men who burned the temple, blinded Zedekiah, and carried Judah to the rivers of Babylon. The second sense is technical: in Daniel the Chaldeans are a professional order, listed with “the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers” (Dan 2:2) — the learned caste of the empire, masters of omens and star-reading, who could not tell the king his dream. Daniel could, and the contrast is the book's argument: revelation from the God of heaven against the entire apparatus of Babylonian divination. The dynasty ends in a sentence: “In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain” (Dan 5:30). And it began, long before, with a call out of Ur of the Chaldees.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Chaldean as pertaining to Chaldea, and notes the secondary use of the name for the class of astrologers and men of learning at Babylon.
webster_full: CHALDEAN, n. An inhabitant of Chaldea, a country of Asia lying on the lower Euphrates about Babylon.
The Chaldeans succeeded the Assyrians in the empire of the east, and under Nebuchadnezzar subdued Judea.
Also, one of an order of philosophers, astrologers and diviners at Babylon, famed for the observation of the stars.
CHALDEE, n. The language of the Chaldeans, a dialect of the Aramean, in which parts of Daniel and Ezra are written.
Ur of the Chaldees was the city from which Abram was called.
scriptures: Hab 1:6
For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs.
Dan 2:2
Then the king commanded to call the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans, for to shew the king his dreams. So they came and stood before the king.
Dan 5:30
In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain.

And Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son's son, and Sarai his daughter in law, his son Abram's wife; and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan; and they came unto Haran, and dwelt there.
corruption_summary: Astrology is treated as harmless entertainment; Daniel treats the Chaldean art as the empire's official rival to revelation, and shows it failing in the one thing that mattered.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 2 is the Bible's set-piece against divination, and it is worth seeing how it is staged. The Chaldeans are not charlatans on a street corner; they are the intellectual establishment of the greatest empire on earth, salaried, credentialed, consulted by the king. And their answer to a straightforward demand is that no man can do it. Then a captive Hebrew says the thing that reframes everything: “there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets” (Dan 2:28). The horoscope column and the app that reads a birth chart are the same art with the majesty stripped out, and Scripture's objection is not that it fails to work but that it seeks from the creature what only the Creator gives. Deu 18:10-12 lists the whole apparatus and calls the practitioners an abomination.

The second thing to name is the answer Habakkuk received, because the modern instinct is to soften it. God said He was raising up a nation more wicked than the one He was judging, and He did not apologise for it. Habakkuk's protest — “wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?” (Hab 1:13) — is answered by a delay and a promise: the vision is for an appointed time, the proud shall fall, “but the just shall live by his faith” (Hab 2:4). That verse became the hinge of the Reformation, and it was quarried out of a complaint about the Chaldeans.
roots_summary: Hebrew Kasdim (H3778), Chaldeans; Aramaic Kasday (H3779); 'ashshaph (H825), astrologer or enchanter.
roots_lines: Hebrew Kasdim (H3778) — Chaldeans, Chaldees; the nation and, in Daniel, the learned order.
Aramaic Kasday (H3779) — Chaldean; used in the Aramaic chapters of Daniel.
Hebrew 'ashshaph (H825) — an astrologer, conjurer; listed beside the Chaldeans in Dan 2:2.
Hebrew chartom (H2748) — a magician, one skilled in sacred writing; the same caste in Egypt and Babylon.
Hebrew raz (H7328) — a secret, mystery; the thing Daniel says only the God of heaven reveals.
usage: “Lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation” — the answer that appalled a prophet.
“The magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans” — the establishment that could not.
“Ur of the Chaldees” — where the call of Abram began.

pos: n. (the empire that succeeded Babylon — the power under which the temple was rebuilt, the wall raised, and a Jewish queen saved her people)
etymology: From Hebrew Paras, Persia; the same consonants as the word peres, divided, in the writing on Belshazzar's wall — a pun the reader is meant to hear.
biblical_def: Persia enters Scripture as an answer to prayer. Babylon had taken Judah captive; Persia sent Judah home. “Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia” (Ezr 1:1) — and the seventy years ended precisely as foretold, by the decree of a pagan whom Isaiah had named a century and a half before he was born. Under Persian kings the second temple was built, Ezra brought the law, Nehemiah raised the wall, and Esther's deliverance was wrought in Shushan the palace. Daniel sees the empire as a ram with two horns — “the kings of Media and Persia” (Dan 8:20) — and its constitutional peculiarity becomes a plot device twice over: “the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” (Dan 6:8), which threw Daniel to the lions and which Haman's decree against the Jews could not undo, only counter. Persia is the empire under which the whole post-exilic Old Testament takes place. It is remembered not for cruelty but for a strange, ordered, unwitting service to the purposes of God — a reminder that the Lord governs by decrees He never asks a king to understand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives Persia as a large country of Asia, and Persian as pertaining to it, noting the empire founded by Cyrus which succeeded that of Babylon.
webster_full: PERSIA, n. A country of Asia, bounded by the Caspian on the north and the Persian gulf on the south.
The Persian empire was founded by Cyrus, who overthrew the Chaldean monarchy and took Babylon.
By his decree the Jews returned from captivity and the house of the Lord at Jerusalem was rebuilt.
The laws of the Medes and Persians were held unalterable, once signed by the king.
The empire was overthrown by Alexander of Macedon, as foreshown in the visions of Daniel.
scriptures: Ezr 1:1

Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing, saying,
And them that had escaped from the sword carried he away to Babylon; where they were servants to him and his sons until the reign of the kingdom of Persia:
Dan 8:20
The ram which thou sawest having two horns are the kings of Media and Persia.
Dan 6:8
Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not.
corruption_summary: Daniel's naming of Persia and Greece in advance is the chief reason critics date the book to the second century; the argument assumes at the outset that prophecy cannot happen.
corruption_paragraphs: The four empires of Daniel are the pivot of the argument over the book's date. Because the visions describe the Persian and Greek periods with accuracy, the standard critical position places the writing after those events, in the days of Antiochus. Note the structure of the reasoning: predictive prophecy is excluded before the evidence is weighed, so accuracy becomes proof of lateness. The dictionary holds the sixth-century Daniel of the Hebrew canon — the man Ezekiel names among the righteous (Eze 14:14), whose book the Lord Jesus cites as spoken “by Daniel the prophet” (Mat 24:15). If God foretells, then a book that foretells is what it claims to be, and the internal Aramaic, the Persian loanwords, and the Babylonian court detail fit a writer who was there.

The second corruption is smaller but worth naming: the habit of reading Cyrus as a model of enlightened tolerance and stopping there. Ezr 1:1 does not say Cyrus was tolerant. It says the LORD stirred up his spirit so that Jeremiah's word might be fulfilled. Isa 45 goes further and calls him by name, “my shepherd” and even the LORD's anointed, and then says plainly, “I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me” (Isa 45:4). A ruler can be the instrument of a covenant purpose he has never heard of. That is a comfort in every generation, and it is not a reason to baptise the ruler.
roots_summary: Hebrew Paras (H6539), Persia; Paras also puns on peres (H6537), divided, in Dan 5:28; 'ur (H5782), to stir up.
roots_lines: Hebrew Paras (H6539) — Persia, Persian; the empire of Cyrus, Darius, and Ahasuerus.
Aramaic peres (H6537) — divided; the third word on Belshazzar's wall, sounding the name of the conqueror.
Hebrew 'ur (H5782) — to rouse, stir up; what the LORD did to the spirit of Cyrus (Ezr 1:1).
Hebrew dath (H1881) — a decree, law; the Persian edict that could not be altered.
Hebrew Shushan (H7800) — Shushan, Susa, the palace-city of Esther and of Daniel's later visions.
usage: “The LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia” — a pagan decree fulfilling a prophet's word.
“The kings of Media and Persia” — the two-horned ram of Daniel's vision.
“The law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” — a constitution that trapped its own king.

pos: n. pl. (the people of Media, north-east of Babylon — the second horn of the ram, and the law that could not be altered)
etymology: From Hebrew Maday, Media or Mede — also the name of a son of Japheth (Gen 10:2), which places the nation in the Japhethite line. The Greek Medos follows.
biblical_def: The Medes occupied the highlands east of Assyria and north of Elam, and Scripture first mentions them as a place of exile: the ten tribes were settled “in the cities of the Medes” (2Ki 17:6). A century and more later Isaiah names them as the instrument of Babylon's fall, and adds a detail that no bribe would stop them: “Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it” (Isa 13:17). It happened. Daniel reads the writing on the wall and gives the interpretation: “PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians” (Dan 5:28), and that night the Chaldean king was slain. Thereafter Media and Persia are named together as one dual power, the ram with two horns, one higher than the other. Their most famous contribution to Scripture is constitutional: a signed royal decree was irrevocable, “the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” (Dan 6:8). Darius used it against himself and spent a sleepless night over a lions' den he could not open; Ahasuerus could not recall Haman's edict and had to issue a second. Medes are still present at Pentecost, listed among the nations that heard the wonderful works of God in their own tongue.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives Mede as a native of Media, an ancient country of Asia, and notes the joint empire of the Medes and Persians founded upon the fall of Babylon.
webster_full: MEDE, n. A native or inhabitant of Media, a country of Asia lying south and west of the Caspian sea.
The Medes were descended from Madai, the son of Japheth.
In league with the Chaldeans they overthrew Nineveh, and afterward, with Cyrus, they took Babylon.
The laws of the Medes and Persians, once signed, might not be changed.
Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old.
scriptures: Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it.
Dan 5:28
PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.
Dan 6:8
Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not.
In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.
corruption_summary: An unalterable human law is admired as the height of legal order; Daniel and Esther both show it trapping the king who made it, and Scripture reserves immutability for God alone.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle worth recovering from the Medes is a doctrine of law. Their boast was a statute that could not be altered, and Scripture shows it twice producing absurdity: a king who loved Daniel obliged to throw him to lions, and an empire obliged to let a genocidal decree stand and merely arm its victims against it. Human law needs the power of repentance built into it, because human lawgivers are fallible and often malicious. What cannot change is God — “I am the LORD, I change not” (Mal 3:6) — and His immutability is safe precisely because His will is perfectly holy. Immutability in a fallen legislature is not majesty; it is a trap.

There is a second and happier thing here. The decree of Darius could not be altered, and neither could the covenant. The writer to the Hebrews reaches for exactly this legal picture: God, “willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath” (Heb 6:17). What the Persian court could only counterfeit — a word that stands whatever comes — belongs in truth to the promise made to Abraham and sworn by God to Himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew Maday (H4074), Madai, Media, Mede; Aramaic Maday (H4076); dath (H1881), a decree.
roots_lines: Hebrew Maday (H4074) — Madai; both the son of Japheth (Gen 10:2) and the nation sprung from him.
Aramaic Maday (H4076) — Mede; the form used in the Aramaic chapters of Daniel.
Aramaic dath (H1882) — decree, law; the unalterable statute of Dan 6:8.
Hebrew 'ur (H5782) — to stir up; the LORD's act in raising the Medes against Babylon (Isa 13:17).
Hebrew peras (H6537) — divided; the wall-word that announced the transfer of the kingdom.
usage: “Which shall not regard silver” — an army that could not be bought off.
“Given to the Medes and Persians” — the sentence read off a plastered wall.
“The law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” — a majesty that became a snare.

pos: n. (a son of Shem and the nation east of Babylon — the archers of the ancient world, broken by prophecy and promised a restoration)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Eylam, probably from a root meaning eternity or hidden time, though the connexion is uncertain; the name is first a person, the eldest son of Shem (Gen 10:22), and then the land his descendants held east of the Tigris.
biblical_def: Elam is one of the oldest names in the Bible and one of the last to be spoken over. Its king Chedorlaomer heads the eastern coalition of Gen 14 — “Chedorlaomer king of Elam” (Gen 14:1) — the campaign that carried Lot away and drew Abram out with three hundred and eighteen trained servants, and ended with Melchizedek's bread and wine. Elam is remembered chiefly for the bow: “Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen” (Isa 22:6), and when the LORD pronounces judgment it is the bow He names — “Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the chief of their might” (Jer 49:35). Isaiah summons them against Babylon alongside Media (Isa 21:2). What makes Elam remarkable among the oracles against the nations is the ending. Jeremiah's judgment on Elam does not conclude in desolation but in a promise: “But it shall come to pass in the latter days, that I will bring again the captivity of Elam, saith the LORD” (Jer 49:39). And in Act 2 the list of nations that heard the gospel in their own tongue at Pentecost begins “Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites” — the latter days come, and the captivity of Elam brought again in the only way that lasts.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) treats Elam under sacred geography as the country of the Elamites, east of Babylonia, named from Elam the son of Shem, and identified with Elymais or Susiana.
webster_full: ELAM, n. The eldest son of Shem, and the country peopled by his posterity.
It lay east of Babylonia and north of the Persian gulf, and is called by the ancients Elymais or Susiana.
Shushan, the palace of the Persian kings, stood in the province of Elam.
The Elamites were famed as archers, and are so described by Isaiah and Jeremiah.
Elamites were among those present at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.
scriptures: Gen 14:1
And it came to pass in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations;
Isa 22:6
And Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield.
Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the chief of their might.
But it shall come to pass in the latter days, that I will bring again the captivity of Elam, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: The oracles against the nations are read as nationalist invective; Elam ends in a promise of restoration, which shows the judgments were never merely tribal curses.
corruption_paragraphs: The prophetic oracles against foreign nations are routinely characterised as the resentment of a small people versified. Elam refutes the characterisation in four verses. The judgment is severe — the bow broken, the people scattered to the four winds, the throne of the LORD set in Elam — and then, without a change of speaker, comes Jer 49:39 and the captivity brought again in the latter days. Egypt receives the same treatment (Jer 46:26), and Moab (Jer 48:47), and Ammon (Jer 49:6). A nationalist would not write that. The oracles are the judgments of the God of all the earth, and judgment in His hand has always had a door in it.

The second thing to name is how the promise was kept. Not by a restored Elamite kingdom — Elam never returned as a power — but by Elamites standing in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost hearing the wonderful works of God in their own tongue, and by the church that spread eastward through those provinces in the following centuries. The prophets speak of nations, and the fulfilment comes in a kingdom “out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation” (Rev 5:9). Reading the oracles without that ending leaves them looking like grudges; reading them with it shows what they always were.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Eylam (H5867) — Elam; the son of Shem and the nation of his posterity (Gen 10:22).
Hebrew qesheth (H7198) — a bow; “the chief of their might”, the thing God says He will break.
Hebrew Kedorla'omer (H3540) — Chedorlaomer, the Elamite overlord of Gen 14.
Hebrew shub shebuth (H7725 + H7622) — to bring again the captivity; the formula of restoration in Jer 49:39.
Greek Elamites (G1639) — Elamites; named at Pentecost among the hearers (Act 2:9).
usage: “Chedorlaomer king of Elam” — the invasion that made Abram a rescuer.
“I will break the bow of Elam” — judgment aimed at a nation's strength.
“I will bring again the captivity of Elam” — a door left open in the sentence.

pos: n. (the great river of Mesopotamia — the fourth river of Eden, the northern bound of the promise, and the boundary of judgment in the Revelation)
etymology: From Hebrew Perath, probably from a root meaning to break forth or be fruitful; the Greek Euphrates comes through Old Persian Ufratu. In Hebrew it is often simply han-nahar, “the river”, as though no other needed naming.
biblical_def: The Euphrates is the Bible's great river, and it frames the whole story. It is the last of the four rivers of Eden — “And the fourth river is Euphrates” (Gen 2:14) — named without explanation because the first readers knew it. It is the northern limit of the land covenanted to Abram: “from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates” (Gen 15:18), a boundary reached only under David and Solomon. Beyond it lay Assyria and Babylon, so that crossing the river came to mean exile, and Jeremiah was sent to bury a girdle by it and later to sink a book in it as a sign of Babylon's sinking. Then in the Revelation it returns twice, at the sixth trumpet and the sixth vial: four angels “bound in the great river Euphrates” (Rev 9:14) loosed to slay; and the water “dried up, that the way of the kings of the east might be prepared” (Rev 16:12) — the same drying of a river that God had done at the Red Sea and Jordan, now done to open a road for judgment rather than for a redeemed people. From the garden to the last plagues, the same water: a boundary given, a boundary crossed in exile, and a boundary removed at the end.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) treats Euphrates in geography as the great river of Asia rising in Armenia and falling into the Persian gulf, the eastern boundary of the promised land.
webster_full: EUPHRATES, n. A celebrated river of Asia, rising in the mountains of Armenia and running into the Persian gulf.
It is one of the four rivers named in the second chapter of Genesis as parting from the garden.
In Scripture it is emphatically called the great river, or simply the river.
It was assigned as the utmost bound of the land promised to the seed of Abraham.
Babylon stood upon it, and its waters were turned aside by Cyrus at the taking of the city.
scriptures: Gen 2:14
And the name of the third river is Hiddekel: that is it which goeth toward the east of Assyria. And the fourth river is Euphrates.
In the same day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates:
Rev 9:14
Saying to the sixth angel which had the trumpet, Loose the four angels which are bound in the great river Euphrates.
And the sixth angel poured out his vial upon the great river Euphrates; and the water thereof was dried up, that the way of the kings of the east might be prepared.
corruption_summary: Gen 2 is read as myth borrowed from Mesopotamia; the naming of two rivers still on every map is a strange feature for a myth, and the text plainly means a real place.
corruption_paragraphs: The four rivers of Eden are the standard exhibit for treating Gen 2 as borrowed Near Eastern mythology. It is worth noticing what the text actually does. Two of the four are named without gloss because everyone knew them — Hiddekel, which is the Tigris, and Euphrates — and two are located by the lands they compass. A myth does not usually anchor itself to rivers the reader can walk to. The account presents itself as geography attached to history, and the flood makes the surviving watercourses a testimony rather than a map of the antediluvian world. The dictionary holds a historical Adam in a real garden, and reads Gen 2:14 as the writer intended it.

The second matter is prophetic and calls for restraint. The Euphrates in Rev 9 and 16 has been fitted to every contemporary alignment of powers in the Middle East for two centuries, with a uniform record of failure. What the text asserts is plain enough without the newspaper: the barrier God set is removed at His word, a road is opened for the gathering to Armageddon, and the sequence is His. The dictionary does not hold dispensational premillennialism — a nineteenth-century novelty absent from every Reformation confession — and does not read the drying of the river as a datable geopolitical event. Read it as the sixth vial: the last restraints coming off before the end.
roots_lines: Hebrew Perath (H6578) — Euphrates; from a root suggesting to break forth, to be fruitful.
Hebrew han-nahar hag-gadol — “the great river”; the standing epithet of Gen 15:18 and Deu 1:7.
Hebrew Chiddeqel (H2313) — Hiddekel, the Tigris; the third river of Eden, named with it.
Greek Euphrates (G2166) — Euphrates; used only in the Revelation, at the sixth trumpet and sixth vial.
Hebrew yabesh (H3001) — to dry up; what God does to rivers to make a way, at the Red sea, at Jordan, and at the end.
usage: “And the fourth river is Euphrates” — a river of Eden still on the map.
“Unto the great river, the river Euphrates” — the northern bound of the promise.
“The water thereof was dried up” — the last barrier removed.

pos: n. (the KJV rendering of Cush, the land south of Egypt — the far country of Scripture, and the first Gentile convert of the book of Acts)
etymology: The KJV renders Hebrew Kush as Ethiopia after the Greek Aithiopia, from aitho, to burn, and ops, face — the land of the sun-darkened. Cush is a son of Ham (Gen 10:6), and the biblical Cush lies along the upper Nile, in modern Sudan rather than the modern Ethiopian state.
biblical_def: Ethiopia in the KJV translates the Hebrew Cush, the land beyond the southern border of Egypt, and it functions in Scripture as the far country — the edge of the known world. It appears at the beginning, where Gihon “compasseth the whole land of Ethiopia” (Gen 2:13); Moses married an Ethiopian woman and Miriam was struck leprous for despising it; Ebedmelech the Ethiopian eunuch pulled Jeremiah out of the dungeon with old rags for his armpits, an act of mercy God rewarded by name. Jeremiah also coins the proverb of the unchangeable heart: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil” (Jer 13:23) — a text on total depravity, not on complexion. Above all there is the psalm: “Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God” (Psa 68:31). Luke records the answer. Philip is sent to a desert road to meet “a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians” (Act 8:27), reading Isaiah 53 in a chariot. He was baptised and went on his way rejoicing, and the far country had stretched out its hands.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives Ethiopia as a country of Africa south of Egypt, and Ethiopian as its inhabitant, noting the Greek derivation from a burnt or sun-blackened countenance.
webster_full: ETHIOPIA, n. A country of Africa lying south of Egypt, called in Hebrew Cush.
The name is Greek, and denotes the country of the sun-burnt visage.
ETHIOPIAN, n. A native of Ethiopia; a blackamoor.
Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a servant in the house of the king of Judah, delivered Jeremiah from the dungeon.
An eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, was baptized by Philip the evangelist.
scriptures: Gen 2:13
And the name of the second river is Gihon: the same is it that compasseth the whole land of Ethiopia.
Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God.
Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.
Act 8:27

And he arose and went: and, behold, a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship,
corruption_summary: Jer 13:23 has been abused in both directions — quoted to demean, and then avoided out of embarrassment; its actual subject is the bondage of the will, and the whole Reformed doctrine of depravity is in it.
corruption_paragraphs: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin” has a shameful history of misuse in Western Christendom, cited to suggest a permanent defect in a people. The verse says the opposite of what the abusers made of it. The point of comparison is not that the skin is bad but that it is unalterable by the man who wears it — and that is the prophet's picture of Judah's heart, not of Cush. The whole force of the analogy depends on the Ethiopian and the leopard being simply what God made them. Anyone who reads a slur into it has inverted the grammar. The dictionary holds Gen 1:27 without qualification: every human being of every nation is an image-bearer, and Act 17:26 makes all nations of one blood.

The doctrine the verse actually teaches is the one modern preaching most avoids: the sinner's inability. Not that the wicked will not do good, but that they cannot — “accustomed to do evil” renders a word for the learned habit that has become a nature. This is the bondage of the will that Luther defended against Erasmus and that the 1689 Confession states in chapter nine: fallen man has “wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good.” A gospel offered to people who merely need better motivation is a different gospel. The Ethiopian in Act 8 did not change his own heart either; he was sent a preacher.
roots_summary: Hebrew Kush (H3568), Cush, rendered Ethiopia; Greek Aithiops (G128), Ethiopian; eunouchos (G2135), a eunuch.
roots_lines: Hebrew Kush (H3568) — Cush, son of Ham (Gen 10:6) and the land of his posterity above Egypt.
Hebrew Kushi (H3569) — a Cushite, Ethiopian; the word used of Ebedmelech and of Moses' wife.
Greek Aithiops (G128) — Ethiopian; used only of the eunuch in Act 8.
Greek eunouchos (G2135) — a eunuch; barred from the congregation under the law (Deu 23:1), and promised a name better than of sons (Isa 56:5).
Hebrew Kandake / Greek Kandake (G2582) — Candace, a dynastic title of the queens of Meroe, not a personal name.
usage: “Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God” — the psalm Act 8 answers.
“Can the Ethiopian change his skin” — the proverb of a will in bondage.
“A man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority” — the far country come to Isaiah 53.

pos: n. (the Aramean country north-east of Israel, capital Damascus — Israel's nearest and most persistent rival, and the province where believers were first called Christians)
etymology: The KJV renders Hebrew 'Aram as Syria, following the Greek Syria, which is probably a shortening of Assyria though the two are distinct. Aram is a son of Shem (Gen 10:22), and Aramaic is the language of the region — the tongue of parts of Daniel and Ezra and the common speech of Judea in our Lord's day.
biblical_def: Syria is Aram, the highland country reaching from the Lebanon range north and east to the Euphrates, and Damascus was its heart. Its relations with Israel run the whole scale. David subdued it — “then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus: and the Syrians became servants to David” (2Sa 8:6). Under the divided monarchy it became the standing threat, and the Elisha narratives are largely Syrian: the raiding bands, Naaman's leprosy, the blinded army led into Samaria and fed, the siege lifted by a sound of chariots no one else heard. Isaiah's ministry turns on a Syrian alliance: “Syria is confederate with Ephraim” (Isa 7:2), and Ahaz's terror at it produced the promise of Immanuel. In the New Testament Syria is a Roman province: the census that brought Joseph to Bethlehem was taken “when Cyrenius was governor of Syria” (Luk 2:2), our Lord's fame “went throughout all Syria” (Mat 4:24), and Saul was on the Damascus road when he was struck down. Antioch in Syria became the first Gentile church, the place where the disciples were called Christians, and the base from which Paul was sent out.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives Syria as a country of Asia, and Syriac as the language of Syria, a dialect of the Aramean nearly allied to the Chaldee.
webster_full: SYRIA, n. A country of Asia, lying east of the Mediterranean and north of Palestine, whose chief city is Damascus.
It is called Aram in the Hebrew Scriptures, from Aram the son of Shem.
SYRIAC, n. The language of Syria, a dialect of the Aramean or Chaldee tongue.
The Syrians were long the rivals of Israel, and their kings Benhadad and Hazael are famed in the books of the Kings.
Antioch, the capital of Syria under the Romans, was the place where the disciples were first called Christians.
scriptures: Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus: and the Syrians became servants to David, and brought gifts. And the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went.
Isa 7:2
And it was told the house of David, saying, Syria is confederate with Ephraim. And his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind.
Luk 2:2
( And this taxing was first made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria.)
Mat 4:24

And his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments, and those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them.
corruption_summary: Luk 2:2 is the standard exhibit for an error in the gospels; the objection rests on assuming one governorship and one census where the evidence permits neither assumption.
corruption_paragraphs: The census under Cyrenius is presented in most handbooks as a demonstrable historical mistake: Quirinius governed Syria and taxed Judea in AD 6, a decade after Herod's death, so Luke has muddled his dates. Several honest answers are available and any one of them dissolves the objection. Luke's Greek can be read “this taxing was before that made when Cyrenius was governor”, distinguishing an earlier enrolment from the famous one — and Luke himself knows about the AD 6 census, since he names it in Act 5:37. Cyrenius may also have held a command in Syria earlier, under Saturninus or Varus; enrolments were multi-year processes, not single days. What is not available is the assumption behind the confident verdict: that a physician who spent two years gathering testimony in Judea, and who names eight Roman officials and gets the rest right, blundered on the one point his readers could most easily check.

The second and more pastoral matter in Syria is Naaman's leprosy, because the Lord Jesus made it a sermon that nearly got Him killed. “Many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus the prophet; and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian” (Luk 4:27). The congregation at Nazareth was filled with wrath, and the reason is plain: He had said that sovereign mercy goes where it pleases, past the covenant people to a Syrian officer. Election is not a doctrine invented at Dort. It is what emptied a synagogue in Galilee and sent the congregation looking for a cliff.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Aram (H758), Aram, rendered Syria; 'Aramith (H762), in the Syrian tongue; Greek Syria (G4947).
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Aram (H758) — Aram; a son of Shem and the highland country his line settled.
Hebrew 'Aram-Dammeseq — Syria of Damascus; the kingdom David garrisoned (2Sa 8:6).
Hebrew 'Aramith (H762) — in Aramaic, in the Syrian tongue; the language of Dan 2:4 through 7:28.
Greek Syria (G4947) — Syria; the Roman province including Antioch and, for a time, Judea.
Greek Christianos (G5546) — Christian; a name first given at Antioch in Syria (Act 11:26).
usage: “The Syrians became servants to David” — the high-water mark of the kingdom.
“Syria is confederate with Ephraim” — the alarm that produced Immanuel.
“His fame went throughout all Syria” — the Gentile north hearing first.

pos: n. (captain of Nebuchadnezzar's guard — the officer who burned the temple, and who set Jeremiah free with a sermon)
etymology: From Hebrew Nebuzar'adan, representing an Akkadian name meaning something like “Nabu has given seed”. His title, rab-tabbachim, is literally chief of the slaughterers — captain of the guard, the same office Potiphar held in Egypt.
biblical_def: Nebuzaradan is the Babylonian officer who executed the sentence on Jerusalem. He came in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar (2Ki 25:8), burned the house of the LORD and the king's house and every great man's house, broke down the walls, and carried away the remnant of the people (2Ki 25:11). He is the hand on the fire. And Scripture, having established that, records two further things about him that are harder to hold. The first is his social policy: “Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left of the poor of the people, which had nothing, in the land of Judah, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time” (Jer 39:10) — the destitute of Judah received land from the invader that their own nobles had never given them. The second is his theology. Standing over Jeremiah in chains at Ramah, this heathen soldier preached Judah's own prophets back to it: “The LORD thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place” (Jer 40:2), and went on to say that it had come because they had sinned against the LORD and not obeyed His voice. Then he offered the prophet his choice: come to Babylon and be looked after, or stay. Jeremiah stayed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Nebuzaradan; in sacred history he is the captain of the guard to Nebuchadnezzar who destroyed Jerusalem and released Jeremiah.
webster_full: NEBUZARADAN, n. Captain of the guard to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.
He came against Jerusalem in the nineteenth year of that king, and burnt the house of the Lord.
He carried away the remnant of the people, leaving the poor of the land for vinedressers and husbandmen.
He took Jeremiah from among the captives at Ramah and set him at liberty, committing him to Gedaliah.
The title captain of the guard signifies in the Hebrew the chief of the executioners.
scriptures: And in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, which is the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, came Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, unto Jerusalem:
Now the rest of the people that were left in the city, and the fugitives that fell away to the king of Babylon, with the remnant of the multitude, did Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carry away.
But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left of the poor of the people, which had nothing, in the land of Judah, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.
Jer 40:2
And the captain of the guard took Jeremiah, and said unto him, The LORD thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place.
corruption_summary: A pagan executioner states the covenant doctrine of the exile more plainly than the priests of Jerusalem had; the church still prefers explanations of judgment that do not name sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Jer 40:2-3 is one of the most uncomfortable speeches in the Old Testament, because of who makes it. Judah had been told for forty years by Jeremiah that the city would fall for covenant-breaking, and had answered with a state religion of reassurance — “Peace, peace; when there is no peace” (Jer 6:14). Then a Babylonian officer, standing in the ashes, gives the correct interpretation of the event: the LORD your God said this would happen, He has done what He said, and it is because you sinned against Him. When the pulpit will not preach the reason for a judgment, God is perfectly capable of having it preached by a heathen with a sword.

The other thing to name is Jer 39:10, because it cuts against a comfortable assumption. The poor of Judah, who had nothing, were given vineyards and fields — by the invader. God had commanded jubilee, gleaning, and the release of debts, and Judah had ignored them until the land took its sabbaths by force. It is a sober thing when an unbelieving power does more for the destitute than the covenant community did. The dictionary rejects the framework that makes economic grievance the master category of Scripture, but it will not soften what the prophets say about a nation that grinds the faces of its poor and calls itself the people of God.
roots_summary: Hebrew Nebuzar'adan (H5018), Nebuzaradan; rab-tabbachim (H7227 + H2876), chief of the guard, literally chief of the slaughterers.
roots_lines: Hebrew Nebuzar'adan (H5018) — Nebuzaradan; from the Babylonian god Nabu, as in Nebuchadnezzar and Nebushasban.
Hebrew tabbach (H2876) — a slaughterer, cook, executioner; the root of his title.
Hebrew rab-tabbachim — captain of the guard; the office Potiphar held under Pharaoh (Gen 37:36).
Hebrew dal (H1800) — the poor, the weak; those left in the land with vineyards (Jer 39:10).
Hebrew saraph (H8313) — to burn; what he did to the house of the LORD (2Ki 25:9).
usage: “Came Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard” — the sentence arriving in person.
“Left of the poor of the people, which had nothing” — land given by an invader.
“The LORD thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place” — a heathen preaching Judah's own prophets.

pos: n. (a dynastic name of the kings of Syria at Damascus — the besieger of Samaria, and the king whose murder Elisha wept over in advance)
etymology: From Hebrew Ben-Hadad, son of Hadad — Hadad being the Aramean storm-god, the Syrian Baal. Like Pharaoh and Abimelech it is a throne-name rather than a private one, and at least three kings bear it.
biblical_def: Benhadad is the name of the Syrian throne at Damascus through the whole period of the divided kingdom, and it is always found pressing on Israel. The first Benhadad is bought: Asa king of Judah strips the treasures of the house of the LORD and sends them to him to break his league with Baasha (1Ki 15:18) — a piece of statecraft the prophet Hanani rebuked, and for which Asa put the seer in prison. The second besieges Samaria twice. The first time he comes with thirty-two kings and a boast: “Benhadad the king of Syria gathered all his host together” (1Ki 20:1), and is beaten by a handful under a promise, because the Syrians reasoned that the LORD was a God of the hills and not of the valleys. The second siege reduces the city to famine and cannibalism (2Ki 6:24) and is lifted overnight by a sound of chariots in an empty camp. He falls sick, sends Hazael to enquire of Elisha, and the prophet weeps as he tells the servant what he will do to Israel; the next day Hazael smothers his master with a wet cloth. A third Benhadad is beaten three times by Joash, and Amos closes the account: “I will send a fire into the house of Hazael, which shall devour the palaces of Benhadad” (Amo 1:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Benhadad; in sacred history it is the name borne by several kings of Syria reigning at Damascus, contemporaries of the kings of Israel and Judah.
webster_full: BENHADAD, n. The name of several kings of Syria, whose seat was Damascus; it signifies son of Hadad, the Syrian idol.
The first, hired by Asa king of Judah, smote the cities of Naphtali and broke his league with Baasha.
The second besieged Samaria twice in the days of Ahab and of Jehoram, and was twice delivered.
Falling sick, he sent Hazael to Elisha, and was smothered by that servant, who reigned in his stead.
A third of the name was thrice defeated by Joash king of Israel, according to the word of the dying Elisha.
scriptures: Then Asa took all the silver and the gold that were left in the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king's house, and delivered them into the hand of his servants: and king Asa sent them to Benhadad, the son of Tabrimon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, that dwelt at Damascus, saying,
And Benhadad the king of Syria gathered all his host together: and there were thirty and two kings with him, and horses, and chariots: and he went up and besieged Samaria, and warred against it.
And it came to pass after this, that Benhadad king of Syria gathered all his host, and went up, and besieged Samaria.
Amo 1:4
But I will send a fire into the house of Hazael, which shall devour the palaces of Benhadad.
corruption_summary: Asa buying a pagan king with the temple treasure is the pattern of every alliance the church makes with a power it fears; Hanani's rebuke names it as reliance on man rather than on the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Asa had already seen the LORD deliver him from a million Ethiopians. When the smaller threat of Baasha came, he emptied the treasuries of the house of God to hire a Syrian, and it worked — Benhadad broke his league and raided Naphtali, and Baasha withdrew. Then Hanani the seer came and said the thing worth remembering: “Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand” (2Ch 16:7). The successful expedient was itself the loss. Asa's answer was to imprison the prophet and oppress some of the people, and to seek physicians rather than the LORD in his last illness. The pattern is exact and it recurs: a church frightened by a cultural threat spends its treasure hiring a political protector, obtains a short reprieve, and forfeits the deliverance God intended to give it.

The second thing Benhadad exposes is how God treats blasphemy about His nature. The Syrian servants advised a second campaign on the reasoning that “their gods are gods of the hills; therefore they were stronger than we; but let us fight against them in the plain” (1Ki 20:23). The LORD's reply through a prophet is explicit: because the Syrians have said this, He will deliver the great multitude into Israel's hand, “and ye shall know that I am the LORD” (1Ki 20:28). Wicked Ahab benefited from a victory that was not about Ahab at all. God defends His own name even when His people are not worth defending.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ben-Hadad (H1130), son of Hadad; Hadad (H1908), the Aramean storm-god; Dammeseq (H1834), Damascus.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ben-Hadad (H1130) — Benhadad; a throne-name of the Syrian kings, three of whom bear it.
Hebrew Hadad (H1908) — Hadad, the storm-god of Aram; the same deity behind Hadadrimmon (Zec 12:11).
Hebrew Chaza'el (H2371) — Hazael, the servant who murdered him and took the throne (2Ki 8:15).
Hebrew Dammeseq (H1834) — Damascus, the Syrian capital and his seat.
Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, rely; the verb of Hanani's rebuke to Asa (2Ch 16:7-8).
usage: “King Asa sent them to Benhadad” — temple silver spent on a pagan alliance.
“There were thirty and two kings with him” — a boast broken by a promise.
“The palaces of Benhadad” — the house Amos saw burning.
